I can guide you through this family and matrimonial legal matter with care. Here is your structured assessment:

### Understanding Your Situation
You have shared a family matter concerning marriage, domestic distress, maintenance, or custody in your city.

### Relevant Legal Provisions
* **The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (Section 13, Section 13B & Section 24)**: Divorce, Divorce by Mutual Consent, and Maintenance Pendente Lite. Section 13 specifies fault grounds (cruelty, desertion, adultery). Section 13B provides divorce by mutual consent upon 1 year separation. Section 24 provides interim maintenance and expenses of proceedings to a spouse with insufficient independent income.
* **The Special Marriage Act, 1954 (Section 27 & Section 28)**: Divorce and Divorce by mutual consent in civil marriages. Governs solemnization and dissolution of civil marriages between any two persons irrespective of faith. Section 28 provides mutual consent divorce after 1 year living separately.
* **Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA) (Section 12, Section 18, Section 19 & Section 20)**: Application to Magistrate for Protection orders, Residence orders, and Monetary relief. An aggrieved woman or Protection Officer may apply to a Judicial Magistrate for reliefs including Protection Orders (Sec 18), Residence in shared household (Sec 19), Monetary relief for expenses and loss of earnings (Sec 20), and temporary custody (Sec 21).

### Your Legal Position
* Under **Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955** (or Section 28 Special Marriage Act), mutual consent divorce proceeds through two stages: filing a joint petition in the **First Motion**, undergoing a statutory six-month **cooling off** period (which can be waived on valid grounds), and final recording of consent in the **Second Motion**.
* Under the **Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA)**, aggrieved women are entitled to Protection Orders (Sec 18), Residence in shared household (Sec 19), and Monetary Relief (Sec 20).
* Under **Section 144 of BNSS, 2023** (formerly Sec 125 CrPC), a spouse, minor child, or elderly parent unable to maintain themselves can claim monthly maintenance through summary inquiry before a Magistrate.
* Matrimonial dissolution is governed by personal laws (such as Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 or Special Marriage Act, 1954), providing for contested divorce on fault grounds or mutual consent divorce.

### Available Options
* **Option 1 (Mutual Consent Petition):** Jointly petition the Family Court for mutual consent divorce under Section 13B HMA with First Motion and Second Motion after cooling off.
* **Option 2 (Mediation & Counseling):** Approach the Family Court counseling cell or pre-litigation mediation center for amicable resolution.
* **Option 3 (Magistrate Relief under PWDVA / BNSS 144):** File an application before Judicial Magistrate for urgent protection and interim maintenance.

### Practical Next Steps
1. Document all incidents, dates, financial dependencies, and communication history.
2. Consult DLSA (District Legal Services Authority) or a family law advocate for representation.
3. In case of immediate safety threats, contact Women Helpline 181 or local police.

### Evidence to Preserve
* Marriage certificate, wedding photographs, and residence proofs.
* Bank statements, income tax returns, and expense proofs showing financial dependency.
* Medical records, chat logs, or police complaints evidencing domestic cruelty if applicable.

### Important Limitations
* Mutual consent divorce typically requires six months waiting period (cooling-off period), which can be waived by court upon sufficient grounds.
* All court applications in matrimonial disputes require sworn affidavits of assets and liabilities as mandated by the Supreme Court.

I can help you with this. Here is a grounded legal analysis under the operative criminal laws of India (BNS, BNSS, BSA 2023):

### Understanding Your Situation
You have reported an alleged criminal offence or grievance involving the disputed amount in your city. Under Indian law, criminal offences are categorized as cognizable (police must register an FIR) or non-cognizable.

### Relevant Legal Provisions
* **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) (Section 173)**: Information in cognizable cases (First Information Report - FIR & Zero FIR). Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence shall be recorded by the officer in charge of a police station. Mandates Zero FIR (recording irrespective of territorial jurisdiction) and electronic FIR. (Historical Equivalent: Section 154 CrPC, 1973). (Historical Equivalent: Section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC))
* **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) (Section 479 & Section 482)**: Bail provisions, Maximum period of detention for undertrials, and Anticipatory Bail. Governs grant of bail in bailable and non-bailable offences. Section 482 provides for direction for grant of bail to persons apprehending arrest (Anticipatory Bail) before High Court or Court of Session. Section 479 liberalises undertrial detention. (Historical Equivalent: Sections 436, 437, 438 CrPC, 1973). (Historical Equivalent: Sections 436, 437, 438, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC))
* **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) (Section 318)**: Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property. Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine. (Historical Equivalent: Section 420, Indian Penal Code, 1860). (Historical Equivalent: Section 415 & 420, Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC))

### Your Legal Position
* Since 1 July 2024, the operative criminal procedural code is the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS)** and the substantive criminal code is the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS)**.
* Under **Section 173 BNSS** (formerly Sec 154 CrPC), police are statutorily mandated to register an FIR upon receiving information disclosing a cognizable offence.
* Jurisdictional boundaries do not permit refusal: police must lodge a Zero FIR and transfer it to the concerned police station.

### Available Options
* **Option 1 (Police Station Complaint):** Lodge a written complaint with the Station House Officer (SHO) under Section 173(1) BNSS.
* **Option 2 (Superintendent of Police):** If the SHO refuses registration, submit the substance in writing to the Superintendent of Police / DCP under Section 173(4) BNSS.
* **Option 3 (Judicial Magistrate):** File an application under Section 175(3) BNSS before the competent Magistrate seeking a direction for police investigation.

### Practical Next Steps
1. Compile a chronological statement of facts supported by documentary evidence.
2. Submit the written complaint in duplicate and obtain an official receiving stamp with Diary / GD number.
3. Track the status through the state police portal or e-FIR mechanism.

### Evidence to Preserve
* Proof of financial transactions (bank statements, UTR numbers, UPI IDs).
* Electronic communications (WhatsApp chats, SMS, emails, audio logs with Section 63 BSA certificate).
* Certified identity documents and written acknowledgments.

### Important Limitations
* Purely commercial civil disputes cannot be converted into criminal proceedings without demonstrating fraudulent dishonest intent from the inception.
* This analysis is for guidance only; drafting formal bail applications or criminal complaints requires verification by an Advocate on Record.

### Your Legal Position
* Online financial fraud and identity theft are punishable offences under **Sections 66C and 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000** and **Section 318 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS)**.
* Under **Section 43A of the IT Act, 2000** and the **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP)**, Data Fiduciaries that cause privacy data breaches or fail to implement reasonable security safeguards are liable to pay statutory **compensation**.
* Victims of data leaks and privacy violations can file a claim for compensation before the State IT **Adjudicating Officer** appointed under Section 46 of the IT Act.
* Victims of unauthorized debits have the right to seek emergency financial lien / **freeze** on beneficiary accounts through the National Cyber Crime Reporting mechanism.

2. File the incident report on cybercrime.gov.in attaching all screenshots and transaction UTRs.
3. Submit the acknowledgment copy to your home bank branch and request an official dispute ticket.

* Screenshots of phishing chats, fake APK links, fraudulent websites, or spoofed messages.
* Call logs and SMS alerts showing debit timings.

I can help you with this employment and labour law issue. Here is your structured legal assessment:

### Understanding Your Situation
Your employer in your city has withheld earned salary, final settlement dues of the disputed amount, or relieving letters, or you are facing a workplace grievance.

### Relevant Legal Provisions
* **Constitution of India, 1950 (Article 14)**: Equality before law and equal protection of the laws. The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. Strikes down arbitrary state action.
* **The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 (Section 5 & Section 15)**: Time of payment of wages and Claims arising out of deductions from wages or delay in payment. Wages must be paid before the expiry of the 7th day after the wage period (or 10th day if more than 1,000 persons employed). Section 15 provides for application to the designated Authority for delayed wages with compensation up to ten times the amount deducted/delayed.
* **The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 (Section 7)**: Deductions which may be made from wages. Strictly enumerates permissible deductions (such as authorized provident fund, income tax, or willful damage shown after formal inquiry). Any arbitrary or unauthorized deduction is unlawful.

### Your Legal Position
* Under **Section 5 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936**, employers are legally obligated to pay earned wages within 7 to 10 days of the wage period.
* Under **Section 15 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936**, employees can claim delayed wages along with statutory compensation up to ten times the delayed amount.
* Withholding relieving letters or full & final settlement constitutes a breach of contract under **Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872**.
* If facing workplace harassment, the **POSH Act, 2013** provides statutory inquiry through the Internal Committee (IC) within 90 days.

### Available Options
* **Option 1 (Internal Written Demand):** Send a formal demand letter to HR and Management giving 15 days to release dues and relieving credentials.
* **Option 2 (Labour Commissioner / Shops Act):** File a statutory complaint before the local Labour Commissioner or Inspector under State Shops & Establishments Act.
* **Option 3 (Labour Court / Civil Suit):** File a recovery application under Section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 or summary suit under Order 37 CPC.

### Practical Next Steps
1. Gather your appointment letter, recent payslips, bank statements, and resignation acceptance email.
2. Issue a formal written demand notice to the authorized director / HR head.
3. Approach the District Labour Officer if settlement is not concluded within the notice period.

### Evidence to Preserve
* Employment agreement / Offer letter / Resignation acceptance.
* Salary slips for past 3-6 months and bank credit statements.
* Email threads detailing pending FnF calculations and follow-up requests.

### Important Limitations
* Civil recovery of unpaid salary must be instituted within 3 years under the Limitation Act, 1963.
* Managerial employees earning above statutory wage thresholds may need to pursue remedies through Civil Court or Shops Act rather than Labour Court.

What was your agreed monthly salary and the total unpaid salary amount?
